newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ fiscal plans exceed parameters, says Cullen.
newsitem.headline: NZ fiscal plans exceed parameters, says Cullen.

text.p: Opposition Labour Finance spokesman Michael Cullen on Thursday said the coalition government would not be able to deliver its policy programme within the fiscal parameters it has set.

Last week the National-New Zealand First govenment released an agreement outlining its spending plans. It limited extra spending to NZ$1.2 billion in 1997/98, $1.7 billion in 1998/99 and $2.1 billion in 1999/2000 above the baselines in the December Economic and Fiscal Update.
The document in several places said: "All funding proposals subject to being considered within the agreed spending policy parameters".
It included a range of uncosted policy proposals.
Cullen said the coalition's costed proposals exceeded the fiscal parameters by $65.3 million in 1997/98, $137.9 million in 1998/99 and $183.9 million in 1999/2000.
He said that would blow out further once the 18 uncosted items came to charge, and the government released post-agreement initiatives -- expected to be released soon in an "addendum".
"There's no great science in this. Labour has merely added up the cost of the promises as set out in schedule A (of the agreement) and compared them with the fiscal parameters," Cullen said.
"The document also makes a whole range of uncosted promises and fails to make any allowance for fiscal slippage."
Cullen said the government would not be able to deliver all of the programme, despite Associate Treasurer John Delamere's statement he was confident of doing so.

On Wednesday Bankers Trust NZ chief economist David Plank said BT's analysis suggested it would be difficult, if not impossible, to fit the extra spending within the cap adopted by the coalition unless the costings in the agreement were too high, some of the policies are not implemented, and/or savings were made from other areas of government expenditure.

The coalition partners agreed "that a budgetary programme prioritising expenditure will be prepared with the consent of both parties, such programme being within the fiscal parameters as set out" in the agreement.
Plank estimated costed spending would leave only $6 milllion next year for the uncosted policies, $89 million in 1998/99 and $43 million in 1999/2000.
His figures did not include the cost of abolishing the superannuation surcharge in April 1998 which would cost just over $200 million in a full year.
